deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no mathematical derivation. It is Riemann's Latin draft of the 'Theses', the propositions to be defended at the public disputation for his doctorate. They accompany the Göttingen dissertation 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse' (1851). The page numbers and the quotations are left blank or abbreviated with 'ec[etc.]', which marks this as an early concept.

Preamble. The dissertation was not written polemically. But since it will also supply the subject of a public disputation, Riemann lists as theses some propositions on which famous authors hold contrary views.

Thesis I (definition of a function of a complex variable). He cites 'p. 16, beginning of art. 12', quoting 'eine veränderliche Grösse, welche allgemein zu reden ...'. In modern terms the definition is: w = u + i v is a function of z = x + i y on a surface T if, generally speaking (that is, except on isolated lines and points), it has a definite value at each point, varies continuously, and satisfies du/dx = dv/dy and du/dy = -dv/dx. Equivalently, dw/dz is independent of the direction of dz, which is the definition of art. 1 of the printed dissertation.

Riemann claims that earlier authors either did not attribute this property (complex differentiability) to functions at all, citing Cauchy in the Comptes rendus with the reference left blank, or did not put it into the definition. Background (mine): in 1851 notes Cauchy distinguished 'monodromic', 'monogenic' and 'synectic' functions, and so treated monogenicity as an extra property rather than the definition.

Thesis II. The theorem proposed at p. 16, art. 12, 'Wenn eine Function w von z ...', is in Riemann's art. 12. That article gives the result that an isolated singularity at which the function stays bounded, or more precisely where (z - a) w tends to 0, is removable. It also gives the consequences that w is continuous with all derivatives and has a power-series expansion. Which of these the truncated quotation means is my inference. Riemann says the theorem contradicts an opinion pronounced by Cauchy in the Comptes rendus, again with the reference left blank.

Thesis III (begins here, continues on 96v). It concerns how a function of a complex variable is determined. The usual methods start from an analytic expression giving the value for each argument. On the next page Riemann claims instead:
(a) If the function's values are given on an arbitrarily small region, its values elsewhere follow. This is the identity theorem / uniqueness of analytic continuation.
(b) He has determined the number of mutually independent conditions needed to fix the function. In the dissertation this is done via boundary data of the real part plus finitely many constants, using the Dirichlet principle.
Hence the usual definition of a function contains superfluous features.
errors: No mathematical errors: there are no computations. The draft is incomplete, with blank page references to the Comptes rendus and to the dissertation.

The cited 'pag. 16 ... art. 12' presumably refers to the manuscript or proof pagination of the dissertation, not the later printed pagination. The definition quoted in Thesis I in the printed text appears in art. 1 (dw/dz independent of dz), with art. 12 restating it in the 'allgemein zu reden' form for a surface T.

results.what: Definition of a complex function by the Cauchy-Riemann condition (direction-independent derivative), valid 'generally', i.e. except at isolated points and lines
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (monogenic functions) and Riemann (dissertation 1851, taken as the definition)

results.what: Theorem of art. 12: behaviour at isolated exceptional points, with the singularity removable if (z-a)w -> 0, giving a power-series expansion; claimed to contradict Cauchy
A function is determined by its values on an arbitrarily small region; the number of independent determining conditions can be specified
results.modern_name: identity theorem / analytic continuation; boundary-value determination via the Dirichlet principle
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 (with Weierstrass for the analytic-continuation formulation)

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematical content is exactly that of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation. The page's interest is historical: a draft of the Latin disputation theses that explicitly frames the dissertation as contradicting Cauchy's Comptes rendus views on the definition of a complex function and on art. 12. This is a nice unpublished documentary detail, not a new mathematical result.

checkable.sympy: x,y=symbols('x y',real=True); u=re(expand((x+I*y)**3)); v=im(expand((x+I*y)**3)); simplify(diff(u,x)-diff(v,y))==0 and simplify(diff(u,y)+diff(v,x))==0
checkable.asserts: w = z^3 satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations, i.e. Riemann's definition of a function of z (Thesis I)
For w = sin(z)/z near 0, (z-0)*w -> 0, so Riemann's art. 12 criterion makes the singularity removable
After removal of the singularity, w has a power-series expansion at 0: 1 - z**2/6 + z**4/120 + O(z**6)

transcription_corrections: Top left, pencil archival note 'Riemann 13' (not Riemann's text); folio number '96' in the right margin.
'exhibita' carries an inserted 'm' above the line, giving 'exhibitam'.
In Thesis I the correction reads 'referrent', written as 'rent' above the struck 'referendam esse existimarent', so the final text is 'aut non in definitionem referrent'.

In Thesis II the inserted word after the struck 'in' and the Comptes rendus parenthesis is 'pronuntiata'. It is overwritten in pencil, so the final reading is 'Cui repugnat sententia Ill. Cauchy (Comptes rendus ...) pronuntiata'.
'(uti Ill. Cauchy. Comptes rendus' is correct; the reference is left blank in the original.
